Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

</document>
response:
This is a much stronger study than the pilot. It has randomisation, outcomes taken from administrative records, measured actual hours and a registered plan, and it reports the main exploratory analysis with appropriate caveats. Most of the arithmetic checks out. One finding doesn't add up, though, and several conclusions need tightening.

## 1. The arithmetic mostly holds

- Strata add up: 7 + 5 = 12 treated offices and 14 + 10 = 24 in total.
- Actual hours: 33.0/37.9 is a 12.9% fall, and 31.2/37.6 is a 17.0% fall, as reported.
- Output per actual hour follows from the other figures:
  - Case-processing: 0.979 / 0.87 gives +12.5%.
  - Counter: 0.886 / 0.83 gives +6.7%.
- Measured against scheduled hours, case-processing would show 0.979 / 0.8, or +22%, as stated. The comparison of 12.5% with 22% is a useful result in its own right.
- One small anomaly in the confidence intervals:
  - If the counter output interval (−16.9 to −5.9) is divided by the hours ratio, it gives about +0.1% to +13.4% per hour.
  - The reported interval is +0.4% to +13.3%, slightly *narrower*, even though uncertainty in hours should make it wider.
  - This may just reflect a separate estimation, but the paper should explain how it was derived.

## 2. The counter-office output fall is larger than abandonment explains

Counter work is driven by demand: the public arrives regardless of staffing. If demand was unchanged, fewer contacts handled should mostly mean more people giving up.

- Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls. That alone would cut contacts handled by only about 4%.
- Contacts handled per employee fell 11.4%.

Something else accounts for the remaining 7 percentage points or so. Possibilities include:
- demand falling in treated offices relative to control;
- people turned away at counters, which wouldn't show up as abandoned calls;
- a shift in the mix between counter and telephone contacts;
- a change in the FTE denominator.

The paper should report demand (arrivals and calls offered) by arm. This affects how the headline −11.4% should be read.

Two related points:
- **Repeat contacts may inflate the output count.** The repeat-contact rate was 11.8% against 10.9%. If repeat contacts count as "contacts handled," part of the measured output is rework caused by poorer service.
- **Abandoned calls are not a registered outcome.** The 6% to 10% figure appears in the text but isn't in the protocol's outcome list or in Table 1. It should be marked as unregistered and shown against control.

## 3. In counter work, the per-hour "gain" is mostly lower idle time

When arrivals are fixed and fewer staff are on shift, each staff member spends less time waiting between customers. Queueing theory predicts exactly this pattern: more output per hour worked, and longer waits for the public.

So "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" (Discussion) is the wrong reading. The +6.7% is largely the public's waiting time turning into staff utilisation. That actually strengthens the paper's own conclusion that per-hour and per-employee productivity come apart. I would replace "more productive" with "more fully utilised."

## 4. Comparisons that aren't difference-in-differences

**Waiting time** (4.2 to 6.9 minutes) is reported for treated offices only. It is a registered secondary outcome, so the paper should give the estimate against control and its confidence interval.

**Quality figures need more detail.**
- The appeal overturn rates (3.1% against 3.0%) and repeat-contact rates (11.8% against 10.9%) have no confidence intervals. It isn't stated whether they are difference-in-differences estimates.
- Appeals lag decisions. Overturns of decisions made late in the nine months may not have happened yet, so "quality unchanged" in case-processing is provisional.

**Sick days** (−29%) are given only as a pooled figure, with no confidence interval and no split by stratum.

## 5. Inference with very few clusters

Standard errors are clustered by office, but there are only 14 clusters in case-processing and 10 in the counter stratum. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to be too small with this few clusters, so the intervals in Table 1 are probably too narrow.

- Randomisation inference or a wild cluster bootstrap would be more credible. The counter per-hour interval, whose lower bound is +0.4%, is the result most likely to change.
- The central claim that "the effect differed sharply by type of work" needs a formal interaction test. A rough calculation from the reported intervals gives a difference of about 9 points with z ≈ 2.5, which is supportive. The paper should still report the test and say whether it was registered.

## 6. Case-processing: a stable output figure may hide a growing backlog

Over the long run, case-processing output can't exceed the rate at which cases arrive. Nine months of stable output could therefore mean the office has spare capacity, or that it is running down its backlog. The paper says backlog growth is a limitation for the 24-month follow-up, but the case-management system should already show it. The paper should report:
- the size of the queue over time;
- breaches of statutory deadlines;
- time to decision.

Two further points:
- **"Little or no measurable loss" goes slightly too far.** The confidence interval runs down to −6.8%. "Could not rule out a loss of up to about 7%" is more accurate.
- **Overtime cost is not reported.** Actual hours were about 3 per week above the 30 scheduled, and the overtime was claimed. It may also have been paid at a premium, on top of full pay. The county's question is about service *and* cost, so cost per case belongs in the results.

## 7. Definitions that need clarifying

**FTE.** It isn't clear whether a treated employee on 30 hours at full pay counts as 1.0 FTE or 0.8. The text uses "per FTE" and "per employee" interchangeably, and the answer changes how Table 1 should be read.

**Sick days.** If the 30 hours were spread over four days, there are 20% fewer days on which to be off sick, so part of the −29% is mechanical. If they were spread over five shorter days, it isn't. The paper should say which rotas were used, or report sick *hours*.

## 8. The meetings analysis

The paper handles this well. It is clearly marked as exploratory, with a confirmatory test registered for 24 months and a suitably cautious summary. Three things are worth adding:

- **There is no baseline.** Meeting time was measured only in month six, so 3.8 against 7.1 hours is a single snapshot. With 7 offices per arm, the treated offices could have had fewer meetings from the start. The interview claim that managers "cancelled standing meetings" is the only evidence that meeting time changed.
- **r = 0.71 across 7 offices is weak evidence.** Its p-value is about 0.07, and its 95% interval runs from roughly zero to 0.95.
- **A rough check of scale.** Cutting 3.3 hours of meetings from a week of about 33–38 hours frees roughly 9–10% of working time. That is the same order as the 12.5% per-hour gain. The confirmatory test should separate meeting time from other working time.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Pre-period actual hours.** The pre-period figure for case-processing (37.9) is above the scheduled 37.5. The paper should say whether pre-period overtime was handled the same way in both arms.
- **Awareness effects.** Control staff knew a trial was under way, so they might have pushed harder to compete or lost motivation. Control output trends could help show whether either happened.
- **Coverage alternative.** For the counter stratum, it would help policymakers to state how many extra staff, at what cost, would be needed to restore waiting times. That is the realistic alternative to the arrangement tested.

## Bottom line

**Well supported:**
- Scheduled-hours estimates substantially overstate per-hour gains, by 22% against 12.5% here.
- Coverage-bound work loses output per employee and service quality.
- In backlog work, output per employee shows no detectable change over nine months.

**Needs work before publication:**
- reconcile the counter output fall with abandonment and demand;
- present the counter per-hour gain as higher utilisation, not higher productivity;
- use inference suited to few clusters, and test the interaction between strata;
- report backlog, overtime cost and the FTE definition.

This trial also directly tests two weaknesses of the earlier pilot: per-hour gains computed on scheduled rather than actual hours, and the claim that the model works in every sector. On both, the findings point the way that review suggested. If useful, I can draft a response-to-authors letter or a revised Discussion.
